content: 1. Strategies to strengthen the linkage between testing, care, treatment, and prevention are essential to improve the efficiency and reach of hepatitis services. This includes integrating services such as HIV care to enhance access and outcomes. 2. Decentralized testing and treatment services at primary health facilities or harm reduction sites can significantly improve access to care. This approach is supported by task-sharing, which involves training and mentoring healthcare workers and peer workers, and by implementing differentiated care strategies to assess individual care needs, with specialist referrals for complex cases. 3. Community engagement and peer support are critical to promoting access to services and ensuring continuity of care. These efforts also address stigma and discrimination, which are significant barriers to service uptake. 4. Efficient procurement and supply management of quality-assured, affordable medicines and diagnostics are necessary to ensure the availability of essential resources for hepatitis care. 5. Robust data systems are required to monitor the quality of individual care and population-level coverage at key steps along the care continuum. This ensures that interventions are effective and resources are optimally utilized. 6. National planning for hepatitis C virus (HCV) elimination should follow a structured approach. The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided a manual to guide national program managers in developing evidence-based plans that align with health systems and universal health coverage principles. 7. Simplified, standardized algorithms for testing, treatment, and monitoring are recommended. These algorithms can be adapted for national use and provide clear, actionable steps to streamline care delivery. 8. Barriers to successful testing and linkage to care, such as stigma, high costs, transportation challenges, and long waiting times, must be addressed. Interventions to expand testing uptake and improve linkage to confirmatory viral load testing and treatment initiation are critical. 9. WHO guidelines recommend adopting strategies to enhance testing uptake and linkage to care in both facilityand community-based settings. Evidence-based interventions include peer and lay health worker support, clinician reminders, integrated service delivery, and the use of dried blood spot specimens for testing. 10. Integrated testing, care, and treatment systems are essential to improve access to hepatitis services. This includes integrating hepatitis testing with other health services, such as HIV, tuberculosis, and sexually transmitted infection clinics, as well as harm reduction programs. 11. The integration of hepatitis testing into other health services can address multiple health needs simultaneously, saving time and resources for patients and healthcare systems. 12. The use of combination integrated serological tests for HIV, HBV, and HCV allows for efficient testing using a single specimen. Preliminary results for these assays are promising, though further validation is needed. 13. Multidisease testing platforms, such as those used for HIV and tuberculosis, can be adapted for HCV viral load testing. This approach increases access and system efficiency while reducing costs. 14. Decentralized service delivery brings care closer to patients’ homes, reducing transportation costs and waiting times. This approach has been successful in scaling up HIV treatment services and can be adapted for viral hepatitis care. 15. Task-sharing is a pragmatic solution to address shortages of trained healthcare workers and specialists. It involves training non-specialists and nurses to deliver care, with access to specialist support for complex cases. 16. Differentiated care models tailor services to individual needs, ensuring that those with complex problems receive specialized care while reducing the burden on central clinics. This approach has been effective in HIV care and can be applied to HCV management. 17. Community engagement and peer-led interventions are effective in increasing access to care, supporting treatment adherence, and reducing stigma, particularly for marginalized populations such as people who inject drugs (PWID). 18. Countries that procure generic medicines and register multiple products from different manufacturers can achieve significant cost reductions, making treatment more accessible. 19. Key steps to increase the availability of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) and diagnostics include selecting appropriate products, determining the availability of generic medicines, registering products with national regulatory authorities, and forecasting demand to ensure adequate supply. 20. Continuity of prevention and care is essential to avoid reinfection, particularly among high-risk groups such as PWID and men who have sex with men (MSM). Integrated service delivery and information-sharing systems are critical to achieving this goal.
